newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire army surrenders to rebels at border post.
newsitem.headline: Zaire army surrenders to rebels at border post.

text.p: A Zaire army captain who saw the writing on the wall ran up the white flag on a freshly cut sapling at this border post across from Zambia on Wednesday, unleashing a tide of joy from ragged villagers.

"Ka-bi-la, Ka-bi-la" they chanted deafeningly, dancing in the dust and waving their arms to celebrate the latest small victory of rebel forces led by Laurent Kabila against the crumbling regime of President Mobutu Sese Seko.

For the past two weeks, as Kabila's men tightened their noose on the city of Lubumbashi about 50 km (30 miles) to the north, cornering Mobutu forces, the people here were afraid to speak out for the change they all plainly crave.

The feared SNIP secret police kept local sentiment in check and units of Mobutu's crack presidential guard, sent from the capital Kinshasa, promised to put up stiff resistance to the advancing rebels whether the regular army fought or not.

When the news arrived that rebels on Wednesday entered Lubumbashi, and a rebel colonel strode alone into his command post, Captain Ptshiateo Ali Lobando of the government forces (FAZ) knew the game was up.
"There was, necessarily, resistance. But it did not hold out," Lobando, 39, told Reuters.

"This afternoon we had a visit. Colonel Kapenda of the Kabila forces came to see us. He found us in a meeting and told us he and his men had been in our vicinity for the past five days. We exchanged views," the captain said drily.

"We had learned of the fall of Kipushi, of Mokambo on the other side, and today the fall of the big city of Lubumubashi. If these big places couldn't resist there was no point in sacrificing the lives of our soldiers so I asked them to lay down their arms."
A patch of white sheet fluttering above the low green painted commando post signalled that the occupants were going over to the rebels.
Leaving nothing to chance, most of Lobando's command of two dozen men also discarded their uniforms and donned white headbands.

When a television crew appeared from the Zambian side of the frontier, which had been hostile to foreign reporters only hours earlier, all lingering uncertainty evaporated and a crowd of hundreds of Zaireans erupted in an outpouring of celebration.
"This country wants change. It deserves change and it's going to have it," law student Nkila Lulu said.
The days of corruption and plundering of Zaire's mineral wealth by the Mobutu clique were over, he added to cheers from a circle of excited onlookers who shook their fists in the air.

For many in the crowd, however, joy was mingled with anxiety. Some asked hopefully if their country would soon see the "blue helmets" of a United Nations peackeeping force, and when told no they looked disappointed.

They had heard of the latest political clashes in the capital, Kinshasa, and appeared to have little clear idea of where these would lead or for that matter what Kabila represented, apart from quite simply an end to Mobutism.
But for the vast majority that in itself was enough.
